title: Encryption in Transit & at Rest
subtitle: Watch one card number get protected on the wire with TLS and on disk with envelope encryption and a KMS.
learn: How a TLS 1.3 handshake uses asymmetric keys to agree on a fast symmetric key
Why bulk data is encrypted with symmetric keys and asymmetric crypto only sets them up
How envelope encryption keeps master keys inside a KMS and data keys next to the data
How key rotation works without re-encrypting everything at once
Why hashing is not encryption and when to use each

steps.title: Who can read this card number?
steps.body: A customer types a card number into the browser. It must cross the internet, pass through our servers, and then sit in a database and in nightly backups. If it is plain text, anyone who can watch the network, steal a disk, or copy a backup can read it. So we need protection in two places: while it moves (in transit) and while it sits (at rest).
steps.idea: Data is exposed in two states, moving and stored, and each needs its own protection.
steps.caption: A card number must travel and then be stored.

steps.title: Two kinds of keys
steps.body: Encryption scrambles data with a key. Symmetric encryption (like AES-256-GCM) uses one shared secret key to lock and unlock. It is very fast: often several GB/s per core with hardware support. Asymmetric encryption uses a key pair: a public key anyone may have and a private key kept secret. It lets two strangers agree on a secret over an open network, but it is far slower (a rule of thumb: around a thousand times), so it is never used for bulk data.
steps.idea: Use asymmetric crypto to agree on a secret, then symmetric crypto to move the data.
steps.caption: Both sides need the same fast key, shared safely.

steps.title: TLS 1.3 handshake
steps.body: TLS is the encryption behind HTTPS. In the TLS 1.3 handshake, the browser sends a hello with a fresh ephemeral public value (made for this one connection, then thrown away). The server replies with its own value and a certificate, and signs the exchange with its private key. The browser checks that the certificate chains to a trusted authority and matches the hostname. Both sides then compute the same session key without ever sending it. This takes one round trip, so on a path with a 50 ms round trip it adds about 50 ms (on top of the TCP connect) before encrypted data flows.
steps.idea: The handshake proves the server's identity and derives a shared key that never crosses the wire.
steps.caption: Handshake finishes in one round trip.

steps.title: Data moves under the session key
steps.body: Now the card number is encrypted with the symmetric session key, using an authenticated mode such as AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305. "Authenticated" means any tampering is detected, not just hidden. Someone watching the network sees only random-looking bytes (plus who is talking to whom and how much). Forward secrecy comes from the throwaway ephemeral values: if the server's long-term key is stolen later, recorded traffic still cannot be decrypted.
steps.idea: Encryption in transit hides data and protects integrity; ephemeral keys give forward secrecy.
steps.caption: Only ciphertext crosses the internet.

steps.title: Where TLS ends
steps.body: The TLS terminator (the server that ends the TLS connection) decrypts the traffic so it can route and inspect it. If it then forwards plain HTTP, anyone inside the network can read the card number. Many teams re-encrypt that hop with mutual TLS (mTLS), where both sides present certificates. The cost is extra CPU and certificate management. TLS protects one connection, not the data after it is received.
steps.idea: TLS covers one hop; decide deliberately whether internal hops get encrypted too.
steps.caption: The internal hop is re-encrypted with mutual TLS.

steps.title: At rest: envelope encryption
steps.body: Disk encryption protects a stolen drive, but not someone who steals a database login. To protect the field itself, use envelope encryption. The service asks the KMS (key management service, a hardened vault for keys) for a data key. The KMS returns it twice: plain, and wrapped (encrypted) by a master key that never leaves the KMS. The service encrypts the card number with the plain key, stores the wrapped key beside the ciphertext in the database, and discards the plain key from memory.
steps.idea: A master key in the KMS wraps many small data keys; only wrapped keys sit next to the data.
steps.caption: KMS issues a data key, plain and wrapped. Only the wrapped copy is stored.

steps.title: Reading it back
steps.body: To read the record, the service loads the ciphertext and the wrapped data key, then asks the KMS to unwrap the key. The KMS checks the caller's permissions and logs the call, so every decrypt is auditable. The service then decrypts locally. The KMS only handles tiny keys, never the data, so a single master key can protect terabytes. Many services cache unwrapped keys briefly to cut KMS calls.
steps.idea: The KMS gates and audits access to keys; the bulk data never travels to it.
steps.caption: KMS unwraps the key; decryption is local.

steps.title: Rotating the master key
steps.body: Policy says rotate the master key yearly, or on demand. Re-encrypting every record would be slow and risky. Instead the KMS creates a new master key version for all new wraps and keeps old versions to unwrap old keys, so old data keys keep working. Re-wrapping the small wrapped keys under the new version is optional and can run in the background. The bulk ciphertext is untouched. If a key was actually exposed, re-encrypt the data it protected, because rotation alone does not undo a copy.
steps.idea: Envelope encryption makes rotation cheap: re-wrap small keys, not big data.
steps.caption: Wrapped key in the DB re-wrapped under master key v2.

steps.title: Hashing is not encryption
steps.body: Encryption can be reversed with the key. A hash function such as SHA-256 is one-way: it turns any input into a fixed 32-byte fingerprint that cannot be undone. Use hashes to detect corruption (did this backup change?). To resist tampering, keep the hash where an attacker cannot write, or use a keyed MAC or signature. Hashes also store passwords, but only with a slow salted algorithm. Never hash a card number you need back later, and a small input space can be brute-forced anyway.
steps.idea: Encrypt when you must read the data back; hash when you only need to compare or verify.
steps.caption: Encrypted backup goes to object storage; its checksum is kept elsewhere.

steps.title: Layers, not one lock
steps.body: TLS uses asymmetric crypto once to derive a symmetric session key, which protects data on each hop. At rest, envelope encryption keeps data keys beside the data and master keys in a KMS that checks and logs every use. Rotation re-wraps small keys instead of re-encrypting everything. Hashes verify, encryption conceals. Managing the keys, not choosing the algorithms, is the hard part.
steps.idea: Pick the right tool per state, and protect the keys more carefully than the data.
steps.caption: Every hop and every stored copy is covered.

quiz.q: Why does TLS use asymmetric cryptography only during the handshake and not for the whole connection?
options: Asymmetric keys are shorter and easier to store
Asymmetric operations are far slower, so they set up a symmetric key that does the bulk work
Symmetric encryption cannot detect tampering
Browsers do not support asymmetric encryption for data
quiz.why: Asymmetric crypto solves key agreement between strangers but is orders of magnitude slower. TLS uses it once, then switches to a fast symmetric cipher.

quiz.q: In envelope encryption, what is stored next to the encrypted record in the database?
options: The plain data key
The KMS master key
The data key wrapped by the master key
A SHA-256 hash of the plain data key
quiz.why: The wrapped data key is useless without the KMS, which holds the master key. Storing the plain key or master key beside the data would defeat the purpose.

quiz.q: You rotate the master key in the KMS. What must happen to 5 TB of existing ciphertext to keep it readable?
options: All 5 TB must be decrypted and re-encrypted immediately
Nothing; the KMS keeps old versions and can still unwrap old data keys
The browser must redo the TLS handshake
The data must be hashed with the new key
quiz.why: Old master key versions remain available for unwrapping. Optionally re-wrap the small data keys in the background; the 5 TB of ciphertext is not touched.

quiz.q: A service stores a partner API token that it must later send back to the partner. Which is correct?
options: Hash it with SHA-256, since hashes are safer
Store it in plain text behind TLS
Encode it with Base64
Encrypt it, because it must be recovered in its original form
quiz.why: A hash cannot be reversed, so the token could never be sent again. Encryption is reversible with the key. Base64 is only encoding and offers no secrecy.

quiz.q: An attacker records TLS 1.3 traffic for a year, then steals the server's long-term private key. What can they read?
options: Everything recorded, since the key decrypts all sessions
Only the first request of each session
Nothing from the recorded sessions, thanks to forward secrecy
Only sessions that used resumption
quiz.why: Session keys come from ephemeral key exchange and are discarded. The long-term key only proves identity, so it cannot decrypt past traffic.

cheatsheet.def: One shared key locks and unlocks. Fast, used for all bulk data. GCM adds tamper detection.
Public/private key pair. Slow; used for key agreement and signatures, not bulk data.
One round trip to verify the certificate and derive a session key. Ephemeral keys give forward secrecy.
Mutual TLS: both client and server present certificates. Common for service-to-service traffic.
Data encrypted with a data key; data key wrapped by a master key held in a KMS. Wrapped key is stored with the data.
Key management service. Keeps master keys in hardened storage, never exports them, enforces access rules and logs every use.
Replace keys on a schedule or after exposure. With envelopes, re-wrap data keys rather than re-encrypt all data.
Hash is one-way (verify, fingerprint, passwords with slow salted hashes). Encryption is reversible with a key.
